A federal judge in California has barred the Trump administration from threatening election workers.
Jude Joffe Block reports the order comes as federal officials have been escalated their feud with California election officials.
In recent weeks, federal prosecutors have warned election officials in California and Washington.
They could be criminally prosecuted if they don't set aside the ballots of voters.
The federal government suspects are likely noncitizens.
A coalition that includes unions that represent election workers sued to stop the unprecedented threats.
The San Francisco based judge acted swiftly within a day.
The judge issued a temporary restraining order under that ruling until mid November.
The Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security may not threaten election workers
or demand they stop processing registered voters ballots.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
Major oil companies ExxonMobil, Chevron and Shell report soaring profits this quarter
as consumers are paying higher prices for gas and diesel.
NPR's Willow Rubin has the details.
Exxon doubled its earnings compared to this time last year.
Shell's earnings nearly doubled.
Chevron's were up 180 percent.
Together, the companies earned just over 36 billion dollars this quarter.
All kinds of oil products have gotten pricier this year.
Due to the war in Iran, less oil has been getting out of the Middle East
and Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries have especially hampered the global diesel supply.
The oil companies gave some of their earnings to shareholders through dividends
and for the most part they're in a wait and see stance.
Willow Rubin, NPR News.
Gasoline remains about a dollar 20 cents a gallon higher than a year ago
while diesel hovers at around six dollars 30 cents a gallon.
Top diplomats from the group of 20 largest world economies
are wrapping up two days of talks in Atlanta.
But there's no consensus on several critical issues.
Divisions most notably over Russia's war against Ukraine
have overshadowed the start of the meeting that began yesterday.
The G20 is not expected to release a joint communique as the meetings end.
You're listening to NPR.
In Poland, riot police secured the Constitutional Court last night
amid protests against the suspension of its top judge.
As Esme Nicholson reports, this is the latest in a long-running political dispute
over the court between Poland's pro-European government and its nationalist president.
The Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw says it has suspended its top judge, Bogdan Svykowski,
who was appointed by Poland's previous administration.
Polish President Karol Nobrowski was mid-flight
and turned back his plane to support his nationalist ally.
Writing on X, at a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.
Poland's pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power in 2023
on a pledge to restore the rule of law that he and the European Commission
accuse his predecessors of subverting.
On X, Tusk admitted this process is difficult, at times even painful.
Nobrowski, a staunch supporter of President Trump,
has refused to swear in judges nominated by parliament.
For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
Trick or treaters in the northeast will have a beautiful day
with comfortable temperatures and no wet weather in the Halloween forecast.
Trick or treaters in the west, however,

San Diego, California, for example,
will likely have its first measurable rainfall on Halloween in nearly 40 years.
The south and the Midwest could also see rain,
but nothing quite as widespread, and temperatures are expected to be mild.
